prompt: The client asks: "Should we launch our ride-hailing app in a new city?" Fact sheet: the city has 2 million people; the incumbent holds 85% share; drivers earn 20% more with the incumbent; acquiring a customer would cost $40, against a $35 lifetime value; entry requires a $5M license; the city hosts a large music festival. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Don't enter: each customer costs $40 to win but brings only $35, and the incumbent holds 85%.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and backs it with unit economics and the incumbent's strength.

options.text: Enter the city. Two million people, each a potential rider, is a big market, and the $5M license is small against it.
options.feedback: It ignores the deciding fact: each customer costs $40 to win and brings only $35.

options.text: Enter the city. Its large annual music festival brings a surge of riders.
options.feedback: One festival doesn't fix the unit economics.

options.text: Enter and outspend the incumbent on drivers; a 20% pay gap is easy to close with bonuses.
options.feedback: Bonuses add cost to economics that already lose $5 per customer.

explanation: Full answer: Don't enter this city. Each customer would cost $40 to win but bring only $35, and the incumbent holds 85% and pays drivers 20% more. The main risk is that the incumbent stumbles and leaves an opening, so the next step is to monitor the market and revisit if acquisition costs fall. What would change the answer: acquisition costs falling well below $35.

irrelevant_facts: The city hosts a large music festival each year.
